I ran out of tool calls before I finished, so these notes are incomplete. I read six sources in full: Enduring Word (David Guzik), Bible Hub's page of commentaries on v. 5, Ellicott's commentary on the whole chapter, Chrysostom's Homily 15 on 1 Corinthians, and a Catholic Answers video transcript. Most of the notes are therefore on vv. 1–8, and v. 5 has the most.

## 1. Traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1**
- "Sexual immorality" translates *porneia*, which covers every kind of sex outside marriage. It comes first in New Testament lists of sins because sex was where Greek culture's morals clashed most sharply with Jesus' teaching. [EW]
- The verb "has" points to an ongoing relationship with his stepmother, not a single act. The woman is probably not a Christian, since Paul never addresses her. Leviticus 18:8 and Deuteronomy 22:30 and 27:20 forbid this, and Cicero treated it as almost unheard of among pagans. [EW]
- In the New Testament, "have" always means actual marriage, so she may have been divorced from the father. Paul says "his father's wife" rather than the Greek word for stepmother because that is how the law of Moses words the ban. The best manuscripts leave out "named." [ELL]
- Chrysostom notes that Paul makes the charge general ("among you") so the whole church feels wounded and shamed. Paul shames the believers by comparing them with the pagans. [CHRY]

**v. 2**
- Paul is more troubled that the church shrugs the sin off than by the sin itself. They were probably proud of being "tolerant." Guzik mentions a rabbinic view that a Gentile convert's old family ties no longer counted. [EW]
- Ellicott thinks Paul does not mean they boasted about the sin itself. He means their general party pride, which should have given way to shared grief and to removing the man. [ELL]
- Chrysostom says Paul faults them for not mourning and not removing him. They should have acted without waiting for their teacher, because the sin was so well known. [CHRY]
- Matthew Henry suggests that party spirit and a false idea of Christian liberty kept the man from being disciplined. [BH5]

**vv. 3–4**
- Being "present in spirit" is not some kind of out-of-body travel. Paul's letter carried his apostolic authority to them. His judging does not break Matthew 7:1, which forbids hypocritical judging. [EW]
- "In the name of our Lord Jesus" was probably the formula for the church's public acts. "The power of our Lord Jesus" means Christ's promised presence and the apostles' delegated power to bind and loose (Matthew 16:19; 18:18, 20). [ELL]
- Chrysostom stresses how urgently Paul moves to stop the "contagion." He compares Paul's presence in spirit to Elisha with Gehazi (2 Kings 5:26). Paul includes the gathered church in the sentence so he will not seem high-handed. [CHRY]
- Poole says excommunication must be done by the whole gathered church, calling on Christ's name, and only for notorious sins. [BH5]

**v. 5** (see section 2 for the disagreements)
- All the sources agree the purpose is to rescue him, not destroy him. Barnes and Poole both say church discipline should always aim to save the offender. [EW] [BH5]
- Barnes, Guzik and Ellicott all point to 2 Corinthians 2:6–7, where Paul later urges the church to take the man back. [BH5] [EW] [ELL]
- Guzik notes that this verse was used to justify torture during the Inquisition, which he says is not what Paul meant. [EW]

**v. 6**
- The "leaven" here is sourdough starter, a piece of old dough kept back. A little spreads through the whole batch, as sin and pride do. Paul is more worried about the church's sin than the man's. [EW]
- Paul may be answering boasting in the Corinthians' own letter to him. He probably wrote near Easter, before Pentecost (16:8), which would explain the Passover imagery. [ELL]
- Chrysostom: if one sinner goes unpunished, others will soon do the same, so the whole church is at risk. [CHRY]

**v. 7**
- Just as Jews cleared all leaven from the house at Passover, the church must remove notorious unrepentant sinners. "As you really are" means: become what you already are. Guzik quotes Spurgeon that salvation is always "from" sin, never "in" it. [EW]
- Ellicott reads the "old leaven" as the attitude in the church that tolerated evil, not the man himself. The best manuscripts leave out "for us," and the verb basically means "slain." [ELL]
- Chrysostom: "as you are unleavened" describes what they ought to be, not a claim that all of them were pure. [CHRY]
- Matthew Henry: Christ's sacrifice does not make holiness unnecessary. It gives the strongest reasons for it. [BH5]

**v. 8**
- Chrysostom, quoted with approval by Ellicott, says the whole of the Christian life is a festival because of the good things given to us. [CHRY] [ELL]
- Sincerity and truth replace malice and wickedness. [ELL]

**v. 9**
- The earlier letter is lost. Guzik thinks letters like it were meant for one church at one time and so were not preserved. "Associate" literally means "mix up together." [EW]
- Ellicott weighs the view that Paul means this same letter and finds it strained. He prefers a lost letter, possibly sent after an unrecorded visit. [ELL]

**v. 10**
- Christians should not expect godly behaviour from unbelievers. Guzik sees cutting oneself off from the world as the mistake behind monasticism. [EW]
- Obeying the command literally would mean leaving ordinary life altogether. The concern is the church's purity. [ELL]

**v. 11**
- Eating together signalled friendship and partnership, so Paul forbids close fellowship with a so-called brother who lives this way. [EW]
- "Idolater" in a believer may refer to the sexual sin tied to pagan worship (compare Ephesians 5:5; Colossians 3:5). [ELL]
- Poole says excommunication ends church fellowship, such as the Lord's Table, but not ordinary dealings like buying and selling. The person should still be warned as a brother (2 Thessalonians 3:15). [BH5]

**vv. 12–13**
- Many Christians judge outsiders, which is God's job, while neglecting purity inside the church. [EW]
- "Outside" was a Jewish phrase for Gentiles. The best manuscripts read "God *will* judge." "Expel the wicked man" uses the sentencing formula of Deuteronomy 13:5, 17:7 and 24:7. [ELL]

## 2. Where readers disagree (v. 5)

I could not reach any of the Protestant traditions' own websites, so I can't report what Baptists, Methodists, Reformed or Lutherans themselves teach. What I did find is that the older commentaries split three ways on "hand over to Satan":

- **Only excommunication.** Putting him outside the church places him in the world, which is Satan's domain. The Geneva Study Bible and Poole compare this to Matthew 18:17 ("as a heathen and a tax collector"). Poole rejects a miraculous reading on the grounds that Paul would not blame a church for failing to work a miracle. For him, "flesh" means the man's sinful desires or his grief, not his body. [BH5] Guzik takes the same line: the church withdraws its protection, and the man's sinful nature (the "flesh") is what gets destroyed, not his physical body. [EW]
- **A one-off apostolic power over the body, not excommunication.** Gill says this was Paul's own act as an apostle, not the church's. It handed the man's body to Satan for suffering. Gill says no one has this power now that the miraculous gifts have ceased, and it should not be confused with excommunication. [BH5]
- **Both.** Barnes, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and Ellicott see excommunication plus bodily suffering, with Acts 5 and 13:11 and 1 Timothy 1:20 as parallels. Barnes and Gill say this power has ceased, and Barnes says church discipline today is moral only. [BH5] [ELL] Meyer calls the phrase the higher grade of Christian excommunication. I only saw a short extract of his note. [BH5]

## 3. Other views

**Orthodox and Catholic, v. 5**
- Chrysostom notes that Paul says "deliver," as one hands someone to a schoolmaster, which leaves the way open to repentance. The man may be struck with sores or disease, as Job was, but to loosen his sins rather than win crowns. Paul sets limits on the devil, as God did with Job ("touch not his life"). [CHRY]
- Karlo Broussard (Catholic Answers) says that cutting the man off from the church and the sacraments leaves him open to Satan's physical attacks, possibly even death. That suffering might bring him to repentance so he is saved at the judgment. He compares 1 Corinthians 11:29–30 and cites Aquinas, who taught that the sacraments protect a believer from Satan. [CA]
